also.hook: Ng did more than any single figure to turn machine learning from a graduate-school subject into a skill anyone could learn online, while simultaneously building the industrial-scale infrastructure, Google Brain among it, that made deep learning practical at big-tech scale.
also.name: Andrew Ng
also.moniker: AI Educator and Deep Learning Pioneer

also.hook: Douglas Hofstadter was born in New York City in 1945, the son of Nobel physicist Robert Hofstadter, and earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Stanford in 1965 before completing a Ph.D. in physics at the University of Oregon in 1975. In 1979 he published Godel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid, a book weaving mathematical logic, art, and music to argue that self-reference and recursive pattern-matching underlie meaning and mind, and it won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction in 1980. He joined Indiana University Bloomington, where he directed the Fluid Analogies Research Group and became a Distinguished Professor of Cognitive Science and Comparative Literature, building computer models of analogy-making such as Copycat with his students. His later book I Am a Strange Loop (2007) restated the argument that consciousness itself is a kind of self-referential loop. Across four decades he has argued that genuine intelligence rests on fluid analogy-making, a position that put him at odds with mainstream symbolic and, more recently, statistical approaches to AI.
also.name: Douglas Hofstadter
also.moniker: Cognitive scientist and author of Godel, Escher, Bach

also.hook: Brynjolfsson has spent three decades building the empirical case for how digital technology, and now AI, actually changes productivity and jobs, work that shifted from academic papers to boardroom strategy as generative AI forced every company to ask the same question he had been measuring for years.
also.name: Erik Brynjolfsson
also.moniker: Economist of the Second Machine Age

also.hook: Hubert Dreyfus was born in Terre Haute, Indiana, in 1929 and studied philosophy at Harvard, earning his doctorate in 1964. While teaching at MIT in the early 1960s, he was asked by the RAND Corporation to evaluate the prospects of artificial intelligence and concluded, against the confident predictions of the field's founders, that AI's symbolic, rule-based approach could not capture the embodied, skillful coping that underlies everyday human intelligence. He expanded this critique into the 1972 book What Computers Can't Do: A Critique of Artificial Reason, drawing on the phenomenology of Martin Heidegger and Maurice Merleau-Ponty to argue that meaning and skill arise from a body acting in a world, not from symbols manipulated in a mind. He moved to the University of California, Berkeley, in 1968, where he taught for the rest of his career and became one of the most influential interpreters of Heidegger in America. He updated his argument in What Computers Still Can't Do (1992) as the field shifted toward neural networks, and his claim that intelligence depends on a body skillfully coping with a world anticipated the embodied and situated approaches that later reshaped robotics and AI.
also.name: Hubert Dreyfus
also.moniker: Philosopher who challenged AI with phenomenology

also.hook: Paul Scharre is a former Army Ranger turned defense policy analyst who leads work on autonomous weapons and AI strategy at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS). He served as a special operations reconnaissance team leader in the Army's 3rd Ranger Battalion, deploying multiple times to Iraq and Afghanistan, before moving into the Office of the Secretary of Defense. There he directed the working group that wrote DoD Directive 3000.09, the Pentagon's foundational policy on autonomy in weapons systems, and contributed to the 2010 Quadrennial Defense Review and the 2012 Defense Strategic Guidance. He holds a PhD in war studies from King's College London and a master's and bachelor's from Washington University in St. Louis. At CNAS he wrote Army of None, a 2018 book on autonomous weapons that won the William E. Colby Award and was named one of Bill Gates' top five books of the year, and Four Battlegrounds, a 2023 book on the global contest for AI power that led to his inclusion on TIME's inaugural TIME100/AI list.
also.name: Paul Scharre
also.moniker: Executive Vice President, Center for a New American Security

name: Authors and Communicators
blurb: Writers, journalists, and educators explaining AI publicly.

reading.body:
The three figures in this category share a function that is easy to undervalue: they created the shared vocabulary and accessible training that allowed AI's workforce to scale alongside its infrastructure.

Andrew Ng's contribution sits closest to the compute chain. Building Google Brain while simultaneously opening machine learning education to a mass audience meant that the people who would eventually run large-scale training infrastructure had somewhere to learn the craft. Demand for that infrastructure and supply of people able to operate it grew together, in part because of that parallel effort. Erik Brynjolfsson's work addresses what happens after the compute is spent, tracking whether AI investment actually moves the productivity needle, a question that determines whether organizations justify the next round of capital expenditure on power and hardware. Tim O'Reilly's role is earlier in the cycle still: naming a technology shift gives industries a stable target to build contracts, curricula, and investment theses around, and his publishing catalog has functioned as a distributed training system for the technical workforce across several generations of infrastructure.

What this data does not cover is the reception or measurable impact of any of their work. The hooks describe careers and roles, not outcomes with attached numbers. The category contains three people, which is a narrow slice of a much larger field, and the data does not explain the selection criteria. Readers should treat these entries as illustrative of a communicator function within the AI ecosystem rather than as a ranked or complete account of who performs it.

profiles.hook: Eliezer Yudkowsky is an American writer and researcher who has spent more than two decades arguing that artificial intelligence poses a serious risk to humanity's survival. Without a formal academic degree, he co-founded the Singularity Institute for Artificial Intelligence, later renamed the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, with Brian and Sabine Atkins in 2000 to help accelerate the arrival of smarter than human AI. Within a few years he concluded that building such systems safely was a harder and more urgent problem than building them at all, and he redirected the institute's research toward what became known as AI alignment. Between 2006 and 2012 he wrote a long series of essays on rationality, cognitive bias, and AI risk that helped found the online community LessWrong and were later collected into the book Rationality: From AI to Zombies. In 2023 he argued in a Time magazine essay that a temporary pause on AI development was not enough and called for governments to shut down large AI training runs entirely. In 2025 he co-authored If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies with fellow MIRI researcher Nate Soares, bringing his warnings about superintelligent AI to a mainstream audience.

profiles.moniker: AI alignment researcher and co-founder of MIRI

profiles.hook: Nick Bostrom is a Swedish philosopher who has shaped how both academics and the public think about the long term risks and possibilities of advanced technology. He trained across physics, computational neuroscience, and philosophy at the universities of Gothenburg, Stockholm, and King's College London, and completed a PhD in philosophy at the London School of Economics in 2000. In 2002 he published the paper Existential Risks, which introduced a systematic taxonomy of the ways humanity's long term potential could be destroyed or permanently curtailed. In 2005 he founded and directed the Future of Humanity Institute at Oxford University, building it from three researchers into a center that helped incubate the fields of AI safety and effective altruism before it closed in 2024. His 2014 book Superintelligence, Paths, Dangers, Strategies became a New York Times bestseller and is widely credited with moving concerns about advanced AI from niche discussion into mainstream academic and public debate. He continues this work as founder of the Macrostrategy Research Initiative, and published the book Deep Utopia in 2024.
profiles.name: Nick Bostrom
profiles.moniker: Philosopher of existential risk and superintelligence

profiles.hook: Ray Kurzweil is an American inventor, computer scientist, and author known both for his technical contributions to pattern recognition technology and for his predictions about the future of artificial intelligence. Born in Queens, New York in 1948 and trained in computer science and literature at MIT, he began founding technology companies in 1973 and in 1976 introduced the Kurzweil Reading Machine, the first device able to convert printed text into spoken words for blind and visually impaired users. He went on to develop optical character recognition software able to read text in any typeface, along with early text to speech and speech recognition systems, work recognized with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation in 1999 and induction into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in 2002. Alongside his inventing career, Kurzweil became a widely read futurist, publishing books including The Age of Spiritual Machines and The Singularity Is Near that argue technological change is accelerating toward a point where machine intelligence will exceed human intelligence. In 2012 he joined Google, where he now holds the title of principal researcher and AI visionary, leading a team working on natural language understanding.

profiles.moniker: Inventor, futurist, and Google AI researcher

profiles.hook: O'Reilly has spent four decades doing the same thing under different names: spotting a technology shift before the industry has language for it, then naming it. 'Open source' and 'Web 2.0' both trace to conferences he convened, and his publishing house has been the technical-literacy backbone for the programmers who built the modern internet, and now AI.

profiles.moniker: Publisher Who Named Web 2.0 and the Open Source Movement
